risk_assessment.rationale: The findings indicate a scanning pattern (type=scanning) with 47 related artifacts and a medium‑severity, high‑confidence risk assessment. No specific phishing technique (T1566), impersonation details, or malicious IP/domain information were identified.

recommended_actions: Escalate to a human analyst for manual review
recommended_actions_freeform_experimenta: Initiate a manual review of the original email content (including any attachments or embedded links) to verify whether the request for audit evidence is legitimate or part of a social‑engineering lure.

Contact the purported sender (jane.tan@meridian-audit.com) via an out‑of‑band channel (e.g., phone call to a known business number or a separate corporate email address) and confirm that they actually sent the request.
Check internal ticketing / audit systems for any recent, legitimate Q2 access‑review requests that match the language of the message; if none exist, treat the email as suspicious.

Search your mail logs for other communications from the same sender or domain to other recipients within victimcorp.com in the past 30 days – a pattern of similar messages could indicate a broader phishing campaign.
Run a sandbox analysis on any attached files (if present) and submit any URLs found in the body to a URL‑reputation service, even though the current enrichment shows no known malicious indicators.
Update your Mimecast policy rules to flag future outbound messages that request sensitive audit data or credentials, especially when they originate from external domains mimicking internal partners.
Document this incident in your threat‑intel repository with the observed T1566 impersonation technique, so future analysts can quickly correlate similar alerts.

If the email is deemed malicious after review, initiate a credential‑reset workflow for any accounts that may have been disclosed and conduct a focused phishing awareness reminder to the affected business unit.
